1) Reception staff give inaccurate advice resulting in calls, online appointments, back to calls, to then be told they don’t decide on process. This leaves the customer to be forced to call at 08:00 for a same day appointment which never exist.
2) Reception staff read out patient details loudly so that customers in the waiting room can hear. This is a GDPR breach, as names, conditions, addresses and birthdates are read out so loudly that anyone in the waiting room can hear.
3) Triaging is done by the doctors. If you by chance ask to see a specific doctor, you have to mention this in the online form and then call the surgery after receiving the notification that your request cannot be fulfilled online.
4) The building is falling apart. The stairs outside the practice have been falling apart since before April 22, which is when I moved to the area. The interior of the building looks and feels like it’s an army barracks building from the 50s. It’s unclean, unsanitary and generally unpleasant.

relative is a patient at this practice. She is elderly, frail, and has multiple co-morbidities, including terminal cancer, for which she is under palliative care. She is also housebound. Over the past month, she called reception several times to request an appointment to review her blood results. Each time, she was given the same advice: to call back on Monday to book an appointment for the following week.

She called again yesterday (Monday) to request an appointment to review her blood results and was once again told to call back next Monday to book an appointment for the following week. She then requested a repeat prescription for her inhaler, which she is dependent on due to chronic shortness of breath. The receptionist gave similar advice — to call next Monday for a GP appointment for the week after.

When my relative mentioned that her legs were very swollen and blue, she requested a home visit. The receptionist suggested that her Next of Kin call on her behalf, despite the fact that the patient was clearly able to communicate her needs. This advice was unusual and disregarded the patient’s situation, as well as the acute nature of her symptoms. She was extremely upset by this encounter and felt dismissed.

As a medical professional myself, I believe that given her background, this patient should have been prioritised. At a minimum, she should have received a telephone call from a medical professional to triage her appropriately. Reception staff should facilitate patient care, not obstruct it.

This is not the first time we have encountered barriers to receiving medical care at this practice. We have previously raised concerns regarding the behavior of reception staff in relation to another elderly relative. Unfortunately, this appears to be an ongoing issue, which is why we have decided to raise a formal complaint, both at the practice level and to higher authorities.

Please bear in mind that patients seek medical care when they are ill and vulnerable. At the very least, they should expect kindness, compassion, and respect. When these elements are lacking, patients may delay or avoid seeking care, which can negatively impact their health outcomes. This is a patient safety issue that requires urgent attention.

We are truly sorry to hear about your relative’s experience and understand how distressing it must have been. We take such complaints seriously and value the opportunity to review our processes to ensure we provide the highest standard of care, especially for vulnerable patients.

Please note, we have not received a formal complaint from you or your relative, and it has been two months since your review. Given the circumstances, it is difficult to treat this as a genuine review.

Regarding your specific concerns, I hope the following information will be helpful:

Palliative and Frail Elderly Care
We understand the challenges of terminal illness, and we have specific protocols to support palliative care patients. Our Gold List prioritises these patients, ensuring same-day appointments if needed. We also provide services for frail elderly patients, including a frailty service run by a consultant geriatrician at Bursted Wood Surgery, which is not part of the universal NHS offer. Additionally, we hold regular meetings with the local hospice team to ensure optimal support for palliative care patients, offer Urgent Care plans, and provide holistic care reviews from our paramedic, Caroline, for elderly patients. Caroline visits patients for holistic care reviews, these are done when requested or when we think one our patients may be struggling and just need extra support. We run events like McMillan Cancer Days, Christmas parties, and offer coffee mornings to create a supportive community, Whilst not a universal NHS offer the surgery has volunteered its space upstairs for this.
  patients can review their blood results by calling the practice between 12:00–2:00 pm or through the NHS app. We regret your relative’s difficulty arranging a review but do provide numerous phlebotomy appointments, including some on Saturdays, which is not universally available.
Appointments
Appointments can be booked by calling the practice, using the NHS app, or visiting the front desk. We open appointment books two weeks in advance, with four staff members dedicated to answering phones on Monday mornings to handle the “Monday rush.” We also offer Extended Hours Appointments and triage urgent medical needs for same-day appointments.
Repeat Prescription Requests
Repeat prescriptions can be requested via email, pharmacy, NHS app, or in person at the front desk. These requests are processed within 72 working hours by a team of four dedicated staff members. Our practice pharmacist handles 28 telephone consultations per week for medication queries.
Home Visit Protocol
Home visit requests are assessed by a clinician who determines if a visit is necessary. We regret any misunderstanding regarding your relative’s request and will reinforce our processes with staff to ensure patients receive appropriate guidance.
Reception Training and Care Navigation
Reception staff undergo mandatory training, including red flags and escalation procedures, with continuous development throughout the year. We monitor calls regularly and provide additional training as needed to maintain quality care at the front desk.
Next of Kin and Dementia Patient Support
We contact Next of Kin only with explicit permission from the patient. For dementia patients, we assess their ability to manage care independently and, if necessary, involve family members to ensure effective communication.
Patient Feedback & Complaints Process
While we have not received a formal complaint, we take all feedback seriously. We value patient input through our ongoing Friends and Family Survey and encourage you to join our online community for updates.

She then requested a repeat prescription for her inhaler, which she is dependent on due to chronic shortness of breath. The receptionist gave similar advice — to call next Monday for a GP appointment for the week after.

When my relative mentioned that her legs were very swollen and blue, she requested a home visit. The receptionist suggested that her Next of Kin call on her behalf, despite the fact that the patient was clearly able to communicate her needs. This is not the first time we have encountered barriers to receiving medical care at this practice. We have previously raised concerns regarding the behavior of reception staff in relation to another elderly relative. Unfortunately, this appears to be an ongoing issue, which is why we have decided to raise a formal complaint, both at the practice level and to higher authorities.

Please bear in mind that patients seek medical care when they are ill and vulnerable. At the very least, they should expect kindness, compassion, and respect.
